data.title: Spanish data watchdog publicises first AI agent-linked data breach report
data.description:
Spanish data watchdog publicises first AI agent-linked data breach report

Reuters
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 9:06 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

MADRID, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Spain's data protection watchdog said it has received the first reported notification of a personal data breach allegedly carried out by an artificial intelligence agent, ‌a case that suggests autonomous systems are beginning to play a direct role in cyberattacks.

The ‌Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) said on Monday in a blog on its website that the incident involved an AI agent using a ​widely known large language model to identify vulnerabilities, gain access to a system and subsequently modify personal data and access invoices.

The agency said that the alleged breach was reported to it by the affected organization and the information remains under review, adding the use of a particular AI model did not mean either the ‌model itself or its provider's infrastructure ⁠was compromised, nor that the technology was developed for malicious purposes.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

AEPD did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment, nor identify the large language model ⁠or the organization targeted by the breach.

The agency said the case was relevant because a third party allegedly used an AI agent to carry out multiple stages of an attack with limited human intervention, highlighting the growing role ​of ​autonomous systems in cybersecurity incidents.

The incident comes as regulators ​and cybersecurity authorities across the United States and ‌Europe increase scrutiny of the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems, even as businesses adopt the technology at a rapid pace.

PRIORITISING PUBLIC SAFETY

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Spain has positioned itself as one of Europe's most vocal advocates of a "trustworthy AI" model that protects privacy, democracy, minors and public safety rather than prioritising speed or profit for the tech industry.

While a single case is insufficient to establish a broader trend, the notification suggests ‌that AI-assisted attacks are moving beyond the theoretical stage and ​are beginning to affect real-world processing of personal data, AEPD ​added.

According to the notification submitted by the affected ​organisation, the agent successfully logged into the system before autonomously searching for application ‌weaknesses. After identifying a vulnerability, it was able ​to alter personal information ​and view billing records.

The Spanish watchdog did not say when it would finish reviewing the reported breach.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The agency said AI does not create new threats. However, it increases the speed, scale and ​adaptability of existing malicious techniques, reducing ‌the time available to detect and contain them.

Controllers, processors and data protection officers must prepare ​for a scenario in which the speed of attacks will continue to increase, the ​agency added.

(Reporting by Corina Pons; Editing by Aurora Ellis)

data.title: Kennedy Center board votes to close for renovations after judge blocks Trump's name from facade
data.description:
Kennedy Center board votes to close for renovations after judge blocks Trump's name from facade

By Bo Erickson and Mike Scarcella
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 9:17 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington

1 of 6
Guards patrol in front of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on the day of a vote by the board to shut down the center for repairs, which means the building will close immediately, in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

By Bo Erickson and Mike Scarcella

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - The board of the Kennedy Center voted on Tuesday to shut down the iconic performing arts venue for up to two years for repairs, a $257 million renovation project that President Donald Trump later threatened to block unless federal courts allow his name to be added to the building.

The decision ‌by the board, which is chaired by Trump and composed of his allies, came less than two hours after a federal judge blocked the center from adding Trump's name to its ‌facade for the second time in five months.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In a social media post, Trump said the renovation work would not start until an appeals court weighs in on the judge's order.

"If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is ​not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.

Tuesday's developments were the latest twists in the saga of the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts since Trump regained the White House, named himself chairman of the center's board and announced plans to reshape its programming.

The center, which is also a memorial to the assassinated Kennedy, opened in 1971 with the world premiere of Leonard Bernstein's requiem mass for Kennedy. It has over the decades been home to the Washington National Opera and the National Symphony Orchestra and hosted such performers ‌as Mikhail Baryshnikov and Wynton Marsalis. It also hosts the annual Kennedy Center Honors, recognizing ⁠the lifetime of achievement of leading artists.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In response to Trump's takeover, artists have canceled performances in protest, and the opera and the symphony were forced to find other venues, while revenue cratered. The board has warned the center's finances are so shaky that it may soon not be able to honor payroll obligations or maintenance ⁠contracts.

Trump's campaign to remake the center is part of his broader effort to leave his cultural and aesthetic mark on the U.S. capital, including a large new ballroom to replace the White House East Wing he ordered demolished, a troubled renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and a planned "triumphal arch" near the nation's main cemetery honoring its war dead.

The center's board has said the venue is in dire need of immediate repairs.

Trump spoke to the board during ​Tuesday's ​meeting, according to a statement from U.S. Representative Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat who sits on the board due ​to her position in Congress. Beatty has sued to prevent the center from adding ‌Trump's name, arguing that only Congress has that authority.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The unlawful renaming drove audiences and artists away. Now the Board has voted to shut down yet again to hide the terrible mismanagement under its current leadership. We'll see the Defendants in court," said Rep. Beatty's counsel, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group in a statement.

JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP NAME FROM BUILDING

As part of that litigation, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington issued an order earlier on Tuesday temporarily halting the center's latest proposal to put Trump's name on the building. The center was named for Kennedy as a memorial under a law signed by President Lyndon Johnson after his assassination.

In addition, Cooper said the board cannot proceed with plans to rename the campus where it sits the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Simply put, defendants cannot install ‌memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress' blessing," Cooper wrote.

Like Trump, the ​board has argued that adding his name in honor of his efforts is necessary to ensure his continued commitment to its ​survival.

"The Board understands that without such appropriate recognition it is unlikely that President Trump will ​provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building and lead the fiscal rescue of the Center," the board wrote in a draft resolution ahead of ‌the meeting.

Trump said on social media that the Justice Department, which represents the ​center, will appeal the order.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Cooper had previously ordered the ​center in May to remove Trump's name from the building after the center changed its marble facade in December to read "The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts." At that time, Cooper also blocked the center from closing down, finding that the board had not adequately considered the financial consequences.

Workers stripped Trump's name from the center in June ​and left the exterior masked by scaffolding and a white tarpaulin.

In a vote ‌on August 13, the board signed off on the addition of an inscription honoring Trump and renaming the center's plaza after Trump.

The 10 options for how the president's inscription ​could be rendered included: "A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump" and "Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump."

(Reporting by Bo Erickson and Mike Scarcella ​in Washington; Additional reporting by Jonathan Allen; Writing by Joseph Ax; editing by Scott Malone and Aurora Ellis)

data.title: US Senator Sanders and Trump ally Bannon call for stronger AI oversight
data.description:
US Senator Sanders and Trump ally Bannon call for stronger AI oversight

By Courtney Rozen
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 9:17 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Pro-Human Assembly Held in Washington to Discuss AI Technology

1 of 6
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) speaks at the first Pro-Human Assembly to discuss AI legislation in the United States, in Washington, D.C., Sept. 15, 2026. REUTERS/Anna Rose Layden

By Courtney Rozen

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Progressive U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a close ally of President Donald Trump, both called on Tuesday for stronger oversight of artificial intelligence, uniting two political adversaries around concerns that the technology will harm humans.

The rare display of bipartisan concern at the same Washington gathering reflects deepening anxiety ‌over unregulated AI, with lawmakers in both parties questioning Trump's hands-off approach even as the technology raises fears about job losses, safety and the concentration of power among a handful ‌of tech companies.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"AI has the potential to eliminate tens of millions of jobs, wiping out entire professions and making it harder for our young people to enter the workforce," Sanders said.

He added, "As many scientists believe could happen, this technology will escape ​human control with potentially catastrophic consequences."

Sanders drew applause from the room when he criticized tech executives for centralizing control over AI technology, including SpaceX CEO and former Trump adviser Elon Musk.

"Last month, we learned that AI has been used for the first time ever to create new viruses. In the wrong hands, this could lead to new bioweapons and a potential global pandemic that could lead to the deaths of tens of millions of people," Sanders said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Sanders called on Trump to negotiate a treaty with Chinese President Xi Jinping at their summit next week to pause AI development.

Bannon, a former White House strategist during Trump's first ‌presidential term, has criticized Trump's approach to overseeing AI, placing the blame ⁠for the president's unwillingness to regulate the technology squarely on tech companies. On his Monday podcast, Bannon said Congress should not pass laws that prohibit states from enforcing their own rules for the technology.

"Here's what we have to do first: to slow down the pace so that we can understand exactly what's ⁠going on," Bannon said on Tuesday. He praised Sanders for the way he summarized the risks of AI and said the country has to rise above partisanship on the issue.

"I don't think you could find any too harder partisans than Bernie Sanders on the left and Steve Bannon on the right," he said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Bannon said Congress will take too long to pass legislation slowing the development of AI. "This is going to have to be executive action," ​Bannon ​said.

He said the U.S. must cut off China from American-made computer chips.

UNLIKELY BEDFELLOWS

Trump on Monday downplayed concerns expressed by industry leaders ​over the weekend about the misuse of artificial intelligence harming people, saying the ‌U.S. already has guardrails in place for the powerful technology.

Backing Trump's position on Tuesday, Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson said there cannot be a moratorium on artificial intelligence development without losing the competitive edge to China and that AI companies can regulate themselves.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"They can self-regulate. They don't need the government to tell them to slow it down. If they want to slow it down, they should," Johnson told reporters.

Speaking to reporters at the White House, Todd Blanche, the U.S. Attorney General, accused Democrats of trying to influence November's midterm congressional elections by politicizing the issue of AI.

The view that regulations will harm U.S. companies' ability to compete with their Chinese counterparts is shared by tech executives, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Dario Amodei, the CEO of AI company Anthropic, speaking in San Francisco on Tuesday, ‌called for better AI safety standards. "Let's invest more in safety," he said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Recent surveys have found majorities of Americans worry ​the technology could be used to eliminate jobs, raise costs for families or otherwise cause social harm.

BACK FROM RECESS

The U.S. ​House of Representatives ended its long summer break on Monday, with members in the House ​and Senate holding private conversations about whether or not to legislate on AI, especially after Trump said there was no need for legislative action.

Congress has been ‌criticized in the past for lacking the collective expertise to rein in or ​regulate technology companies.

Speaking to Reuters, Republican Senator Bernie ​Moreno of Ohio said, "This process of legislating takes so long. Imagine AI four years in. We're dealing with stuff that isn't even relevant in four years."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Residents in several states have also challenged proposals for new data centers, a critical component of the AI boom. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published in June, 77% of Americans worry AI-driven data centers will raise electricity ​costs.

Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon captured public attention last week when he said ‌he resigned from the company, in part because the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."

Also on Tuesday, Andrew ​Ferguson, the chairman of the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, expressed suspicions over AI companies seeking antitrust exemptions while they also lobby for new regulations.

(Reporting by Courtney Rozen. Additional ​reporting by Tim Reid, Alexandra Alper and Richard Cowan. Editing by David Gregorio, Nick Zieminski and Sanjeev Miglani)

data.title: Pennsylvania measles-associated deaths climb to four as outbreak grows
data.description:
Pennsylvania measles-associated deaths climb to four as outbreak grows

By Sriparna Roy and Kamal Choudhury
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 9:16 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Sriparna Roy and Kamal Choudhury

Sept 15 (Reuters) - The Pennsylvania Department of Health on Tuesday reported two more measles-associated deaths, both in unvaccinated individuals, bringing the state's total fatalities linked to the disease outbreak to four.

One individual lived in Jefferson County, ‌while the other lived in Mifflin County, the department said, without disclosing any additional details, citing patient privacy. On Sunday, Jefferson County ‌announced that a 40-year-old woman had died of measles complications.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Pennsylvania health officials have notified CDC of two additional deaths involving individuals who had measles, a spokesperson for the agency told Reuters, ​adding that it is in contact with state health officials as they continue to assess these deaths.

Pennsylvania said last month two residents died after contracting measles, the first such deaths this year in the U.S.

The issue has become politicized as the governor of Pennsylvania Josh Shapiro and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have publicly argued over the cases. Kennedy has said only one of the deaths was due to measles.

In a post on social media platform ‌X on Tuesday, Kennedy said the CDC would include ⁠measles-related deaths in its tally once the National Center for Health Statistics determines measles was the underlying cause based on state-submitted death records.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Kennedy also accused Shapiro of politicizing the response and declining federal assistance, saying the government had ⁠offered to deploy CDC epidemiologists through its Epi-Aid program to help manage the outbreak.

The CDC currently does not include the 2026 deaths in its measles tally and its website says it is reevaluating how it classifies measles deaths.

Kennedy asked CDC Director, Erica Schwartz, to remove a reference to the two deaths from the agency's online ​measles ​tally, Reuters reported earlier this month.

William Moss, an epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg ​School of Public Health, cautioned against letting disputes over ‌death classifications overshadowing the clinical reality of the virus.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Classifying measles deaths can be complex because the virus can trigger complications that ultimately cause death, Moss said. "But we certainly do not want measles deaths to be politicized. They're tragic enough for the family and community."

U.S. MEASLES CASES SURGE

In 2026, the U.S. has had 3,294 confirmed measles cases through September 10, according to CDC data. Pennsylvania has been the hardest hit with 693 cases in 38 counties.

The Pennsylvania health department said it conducted rigorous investigations with cooperation from the Jefferson and Mifflin County coroner's offices to determine that these cases met the ‌criteria to be considered measles-associated deaths before announcing them.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It reports a "measles-associated death" when an ​individual with an active case of measles dies and meets a set of criteria.

Those include ​death within 30 days of symptom onset in an individual with ​clinical evidence of a measles infection and a positive laboratory test, and it is not due to unrelated causes ‌such as an accident. Whether an individual was exposed to ​measles prior to their death or supporting ​medical records are also considered.

Measles, which can cause symptoms including fever, rash and respiratory issues, is highly contagious but easily preventable with the measles, mumps and rubella combination vaccine — a routine shot for children that is 97% effective in preventing infection after two doses.

Americans' trust ​in vaccines for deadly childhood diseases, including measles, has ‌fallen in recent years, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

President Donald Trump last month unveiled an executive order that criticized the measles, ​mumps and rubella vaccine, calling for the long-used combination shot to be split up into three separate shots.

(Reporting by Sriparna Roy ​and Kamal Choudhury in Bengaluru; Editing by Shilpi Majumdar and Tasim Zahid)

data.title: Trump blasts Supreme Court justices over 'horrible' mail vote ruling
data.description:
Trump blasts Supreme Court justices over 'horrible' mail vote ruling

Danny KEMP and Frankie TAGGART
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 8:55 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

US President Donald Trump assailed the Supreme Court on Tuesday after it blocked his plan to restrict mail-in ballots, launching a rare and blistering attack on the justices he hand-picked in his first term.

Trump accused the court of allowing itself to be cowed by Democrats following the ruling, which comes as a blow to Republican hopes of keeping control of Congress in November's midterm elections.

"These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves," Trump said on his Truth Social network.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump appointed three Supreme Court justices in his first term, Amy Coney Barrett, Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch, giving the court a conservative supermajority.

But in his lengthy social media diatribe, the 80-year-old Republican now blamed them for some of the most "destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country's history."

"The Supreme Court has really let our Country down! Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America," he said.

- 'Very frustrated' -

US Attorney General Todd Blanche -- who was formerly Trump's personal lawyer during a string of civil and criminal cases -- defended the president's attack on the judiciary.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"He is very frustrated," Blanche told reporters at a press conference in the White House Rose Garden. "He has every right, and indeed he should communicate his concerns with the Supreme Court whenever he has them."

Blanche added that the Trump administration could continue to pursue mail-in voting changes despite the court ruling.

Trump signed an executive order in March requiring the compilation of lists of eligible voters and requiring the US Postal Service to deliver ballots only to voters who are on the lists.

He says without evidence that mail-in ballots are vulnerable to fraud, falsely blaming them for his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But his plan faced multiple challenges and the Supreme Court on Monday denied Trump's request to lift an order halting it.

Kavanaugh, in a concurring opinion with the majority, said Trump's plan may ultimately be legal in the long run, but "state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections."

Only two of the six conservative justices -- Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito -- on the nine-member panel offered a dissent.

- 'Highly political' -

Trump called the decision itself "horrible" and "highly political."

"It is not easy for me to write this criticism of the United States Supreme Court -- it will likely cost me dearly for years to come -- but I feel it my obligation and duty, as President, to do so for the America we love!" he added.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Democrats hailed the court ruling.

"Trump's scheme was so on-the-nose, so un-American, so flagrantly unconstitutional that the MAGA Court had no choice but to make the right call," Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Tuesday.

Despite denouncing mail-in voting as corrupt, Trump has previously used it himself, including to vote in Florida's Republican primary last month.

The mail-in fight comes with high political stakes ahead of the November 3 elections.

Republicans hold narrow congressional majorities, but Democrats are favored to capture the House and possibly the Senate as Trump's approval ratings remain weak and voters voice frustration over living costs and the war with Iran.

Losing control of Congress could not only stymie the last two years of Trump's legislative agenda but also expose the president to a third impeachment by Democrats.

Ukraine's Zelenskiy says Russian drones attacked Moldova twice while he was in transit

Reuters

Sept 15 (Reuters) - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in an interview broadcast on Tuesday that Russian drones attacked Moldovan ‌airspace twice while he was in the country aboard his ‌aircraft in transit.

Zelenskiy told the U.S. television network CBS that he was in ​Moldova on Ukraine's western border, at Chisinau airport, on his way to and from a trip abroad when the incidents occurred.

"In Moldova, my presidential jet was there and that's why they attacked Moldova, the ‌airspace of Moldova. Maybe they ⁠didn't want to attack me personally...," Zelenskiy said.

"When we came back home, again through Chisinau, again they ⁠did the same."

On September 9, a Moldovan government spokesperson said the departure of Zelenskiy's aircraft for Norway was delayed as Moldovan authorities closed ​the country's ​airspace over a drone alert.

Two ​Russian drones entered Moldovan airspace ‌on that day. One landed in a field north of the capital, triggering a fire, while the second carried on into Romanian airspace.

Zelenskiy had not previously spoken of the second incident.

It was not clear exactly when the president was again in transit in Moldova ‌on his way back to Ukraine from ​Canada.

Moldovan authorities said two drones entered ​the country's airspace on ​Monday, September 14 for about 10 minutes each over ‌the space of an hour before ​noon local time.

On ​Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train on Ukraine's border with NATO member Poland, shortly after former British Prime ​Minister Boris Johnson ‌and other European diplomats had used the same line.

data.title: Iran War Has Cost Pentagon $38 Billion And Counting, Budget Office Finds
data.description:
Iran War Has Cost Pentagon $38 Billion And Counting, Budget Office Finds

Dave Jamieson
Updated Tue, 15 September 2026 at 8:52 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The Congressional Budget Office has put a price tag on President Donald Trump's war in Iran: $38 billion and counting.

That's according to an estimate the nonpartisan office provided to lawmakers Tuesday, evaluating the conflict's cost to the Pentagon. The figure includes the expense of replacing munitions and equipment lost while fighting, as well as the additional cost of fuel and flight time.

Politics: Iran War Cost Tracker Reveals War's Hit To American Pocketbooks

The war, which began Feb. 28, could cost anywhere from $2 to $3 billion per month moving forward — a high price for what Trump insists is not a war but a "small potatoes" conflict.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"As the conflict persists, [the Pentagon's] costs will continue to increase — slowly if the level of violence remains low and sporadic (as it did in May and June) and rapidly if the intensity of the conflict escalates (as it did in July)," the letter from CBO Director Phillip Swagel concluded.

The office said its analysis was hamstrung by the fact that the Defense Department didn't respond to its requests for information, leaving researchers to rely on government and press reports.

Crucially, the $38 billion tab does not include the additional costs that U.S. consumers are bearing due to inflation caused by the war. Iran's throttling of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed gasoline and diesel prices into record territory, rippling through the consumer economy and leading to higher prices in grocery stores.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Inflation has been "the main economic impact" of the war, Swagel noted, with one price index being .5% higher than he would have estimated in February. Although the report does not put a specific figure on the added fuel costs, researchers from Brown University estimate the burden for U.S. consumers to be $107 billion and counting due to higher gas and diesel prices.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

When the U.S. and Israel began the war, Trump said the conflict would be over in a matter of weeks. More than six months later, he is struggling to find a way out as his approval rating has cratered, leaving Republicans facing the possibility of losing both the House and Senate in this fall's midterm elections.

Politics: JD Vance Gets Taunted By A Heckler In A Deep-Red State, Handles It Poorly

Trump has tried to downplay the significance of the war, in which 18 U.S. service members have been killed and more than 700 have been injured.

"I call it a military conflict because it's small potatoes for us. It's not a big thing," he said earlier this month. "We did Venezuela, and we did this. In Venezuela, we lost nobody, and this we lost 18 people. In Vietnam, you lost 100,000 people, and in other conflicts you lost tens of thousands of people."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The CBO also found that the war in Iran has hurt the military's readiness for other potential conflicts.

"The main opportunity cost of the conflict thus far has been the large expenditure of missile defense interceptors, which will leave the United States with a reduced inventory of interceptors for several years," the letter states.

It added, "The shortfall would become especially problematic if a conflict arose with an opponent whose arsenal included large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles."

data.title: Markets on edge as US Fed meets to tackle high inflation
data.description:
Oil prices jumped, US bond yields rallied and equities retreated Tuesday as the Federal Reserve looked set to raise interest rates, with high inflation and AI concerns dominating market sentiment.

Brent crude futures again pushed towards $110 a barrel, while average diesel prices in the United States struck a record high of just under $6.27 a gallon, heaping pressure on President Donald Trump ahead of midterm congressional elections.

"There's no let-up in the volatility rippling through financial markets, with energy prices staying painfully elevated and worries swirling about the knock-on effect for inflation and interest rates," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.

The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note hit 5.03 percent, a level last seen in 2007 before the global financial crisis, as investors price in a likely hike in US interest rates.

The US Federal Reserve began a rate-setting meeting Tuesday with markets expecting policymakers to pull the trigger on a hike to tackle persistently high consumer prices in the world's biggest economy.

Market expectations for a 25-basis-point rate increase have risen sharply after official data published last week showed US annual inflation remaining far above the Fed's target.

With the crisis in the Middle East showing little sign of abating and Yemen's Houthi rebels taking control of a crucial outlet for shipping, crude has spiked this month to more than $100 a barrel.

The surge in energy costs has ramped up pressure on central banks to raise borrowing costs.

The European Central Bank last week lifted interest rates in the eurozone.

The Bank of England is forecast to maintain its benchmark rate on Thursday as the UK economy struggles for growth.

Major Wall Street indices spent the session in the red following losses in Europe and Asia. The broad-based S&P 500 finished down 0.5 percent.

"The heavier cost of capital, rising fuel charges and worries about the potentially adverse societal impact of AI's rapid adoption have pushed stocks to their weakest prices in roughly six weeks ahead of tomorrow's Fed decision," said a note from Jose Torres of Interactive Brokers.

If Fed policymakers vote to hike on Wednesday, it will be the first time the Fed has raised rates since 2023, when the central bank was still battling post-pandemic inflation.

Such a move will be sure to anger Trump, who has launched an unprecedented campaign to pressure the independent central bank to lower rates in order to spur economic activity.
